meta.titre: Genetics and Inheritance: Crosses, Ratios and Lethal Genes

sections.contenu_markdown: A goat breeder at Mankon market pays 45,000 FCFA for a young buck, hoping that its kids will all carry the coat colour that buyers like. Instead, some litters show colours neither parent had, and in other families some kids never survive to birth. These patterns are not luck: they follow rules of inheritance that Mendel discovered with peas and that geneticists have extended since. The GCE examiners return to this topic every year, asking you to define terms, draw genetic diagrams and explain why some ratios depart from the familiar 3:1.

items: Body cells are diploid: chromosomes occur in homologous pairs, one of each pair from each parent.
Meiosis produces haploid gametes, so a gamete contains one chromosome of each homologous pair.
A gene is a length of DNA that codes for one polypeptide, and it occupies a fixed position (locus) on a chromosome.
Fertilisation is the fusion of two haploid gametes and restores the diploid number.

sections.titre: Alleles, segregation and modified Mendelian ratios
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Key terms.** An *allele* is one alternative form of a gene. The *genotype* is the combination of alleles an individual carries and the *phenotype* is the observable characteristic that results from the genotype and the environment. An individual is *homozygous* when its two alleles are identical and *heterozygous* when they differ. A *dominant* allele is expressed in the phenotype of a heterozygote; a *recessive* allele is expressed only when no dominant allele is present.

**Segregation.** The two alleles of a gene separate during meiosis (Mendel's first law), so every gamete carries only one allele of each gene. Fertilisation then combines gametes at random. A Punnett square or a genetic diagram lists parental genotypes, gametes, offspring genotypes and offspring phenotypes.

| Cross | Parental gametes | Offspring genotypes | Offspring phenotypes |
|---|---|---|---|
| $TT \times tt$ | $T$ ; $t$ | all $Tt$ | all tall |
| $Tt \times Tt$ | $T$, $t$ ; $T$, $t$ | $1\,TT : 2\,Tt : 1\,tt$ | $3$ tall : $1$ dwarf |
| $Tt \times tt$ (test cross) | $T$, $t$ ; $t$ | $1\,Tt : 1\,tt$ | $1$ tall : $1$ dwarf |

A *test cross* is a cross between an individual showing the dominant phenotype and a homozygous recessive individual. Any recessive offspring prove that the tested parent was heterozygous; no recessive offspring among many suggests it was homozygous dominant.

**Probability.** A ratio such as 3:1 is the probability of each outcome at every fertilisation, not a guaranteed count. Each fertilisation is independent, so small families can depart widely from the expected ratio, and only large samples approach it. Probabilities of independent events multiply: the chance of two offspring both being $tt$ from $Tt \times Tt$ is $\frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{4}$.

**When the ratio is not 3:1.** Many genes do not show simple dominance. The three cases examined most often are codominance, incomplete dominance and lethal alleles; each changes the expected phenotype ratio even though segregation still follows Mendel's first law.

variantes.quand_utiliser: Use when the heterozygote shows the phenotypes of both alleles at once, or when a gene has more than two alleles in the population.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
**Codominance:** both alleles of a heterozygote are fully and separately expressed; neither masks the other. In roan cattle a red parent ($C^RC^R$) crossed with a white parent ($C^WC^W$) gives roan calves ($C^RC^W$) with red hairs and white hairs side by side.

**Multiple alleles:** a gene can have three or more alleles in a population although each individual carries only two. The ABO blood group gene has alleles $I^A$, $I^B$ and $i$; $I^A$ and $I^B$ are codominant and both are dominant to $i$.

| Blood group | Possible genotypes |
|---|---|
| A | $I^AI^A$ or $I^Ai$ |
| B | $I^BI^B$ or $I^Bi$ |
| AB | $I^AI^B$ |
| O | $ii$ |

A cross $I^Ai \times I^Bi$ gives groups AB, A, B and O in the ratio 1 : 1 : 1 : 1.

variantes.quand_utiliser: Use when the heterozygote has a phenotype intermediate between the two homozygotes.
variantes.contenu_markdown: In *incomplete dominance* neither allele is completely dominant, so the heterozygote shows a blended, intermediate phenotype. In the four o'clock plant a red-flowered plant ($C^RC^R$) crossed with a white-flowered plant ($C^WC^W$) gives only pink-flowered plants ($C^RC^W$). Crossing two pink plants gives red, pink and white in the ratio $1 : 2 : 1$, so the phenotype ratio equals the genotype ratio. This differs from codominance, where the heterozygote shows both parental phenotypes separately. Pink plants never breed true, because they always produce all three types.

variantes.quand_utiliser: Use when a cross gives fewer offspring than expected or a 2:1 ratio instead of 3:1.
variantes.contenu_markdown: A *lethal gene* (lethal allele) is one whose expression causes the death of the organism, usually in the homozygous condition and often before birth. The zygotes are still formed in the ratio $1 : 2 : 1$, but the homozygous lethal class dies, so the survivors show a ratio of $2 : 1$ and the litter or clutch is one quarter smaller than expected. In yellow mice the allele $Y$ gives a yellow coat and is dominant for colour, but two copies of $Y$ are lethal; the cross $Yy \times Yy$ therefore never produces true-breeding yellow mice. Fewer offspring than expected and a 2:1 ratio are the signs of a lethal allele.

sections.enonce_markdown:
In a mouse colony the allele $Y$ gives a yellow coat and is dominant to the allele $y$ for grey coat. Mice with genotype $YY$ die as embryos. A breeder mates many pairs of yellow mice and in total records 240 live pups.

(a) State the genotype of each parent and of the gametes they produce.
(b) Draw a genetic diagram to predict the genotypes of the zygotes.
(c) Calculate how many pups of each colour were born and how many embryos died, assuming the zygotes were formed in the expected ratio.

etapes.justification: A yellow mouse has at least one $Y$; $YY$ mice die as embryos, so a living yellow parent can only be heterozygous.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Both parents are $Yy$. Each produces two kinds of gamete: $Y$ and $y$ in equal numbers.

etapes.action: Complete the Punnett square for fertilisation.
etapes.justification: Each of the two gametes of one parent can fuse with each of the two gametes of the other, giving four equally likely zygotes.
$YY$ embryos die before birth and are not counted among the live pups.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Surviving pups: $2\,Yy$ (yellow) and $1\,yy$ (grey), so $\frac{3}{4}$ of the zygotes survive and the phenotype ratio is yellow : grey $= 2 : 1$.

etapes.action: Find the total number of zygotes.
etapes.justification: The 240 live pups are $\frac{3}{4}$ of all zygotes, so the total is 240 divided by $\frac{3}{4}$.

etapes.action: Share the zygotes among the classes.
etapes.justification: Yellow pups are $\frac{2}{4}$ of the zygotes, grey pups $\frac{1}{4}$ and dead embryos $\frac{1}{4}$.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Yellow: $320 \times \frac{2}{4} = 160$. Grey: $320 \times \frac{1}{4} = 80$. Dead embryos: $320 \times \frac{1}{4} = 80$. Check: $160 + 80 = 240$ live pups.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The colony produced about **160 yellow pups, 80 grey pups and 80 dead embryos**. The live offspring are in the ratio 2 : 1 instead of 3 : 1 because the homozygous $YY$ class is lethal.

items.erreur_markdown: Because $Aa \times Aa$ gives a 3 : 1 ratio, a family of four children must contain exactly three with the dominant trait and one with the recessive trait.
items.pourquoi_faux: A Mendelian ratio is a probability applied separately to each fertilisation, and each fertilisation is independent of the others.
items.correction_markdown: For each child the chance of the dominant phenotype is $\frac{3}{4}$. In a family of four the chance of exactly three dominant children is $4 \times (\frac{3}{4})^3 \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{27}{64}$, about 42%, so the exact 3 : 1 split occurs in fewer than half of such families.

items.erreur_markdown: A dominant allele is stronger, or more common in the population, than a recessive allele.
items.pourquoi_faux: Dominance describes only which allele is expressed in the heterozygote. It says nothing about strength or frequency; some dominant alleles are rare and some recessive alleles are very common.
items.correction_markdown: Define dominance by expression: the allele whose effect appears in the phenotype of the heterozygote.

items.erreur_markdown: A parent of genotype $Tt$ produces gametes $Tt$, $TT$ and $tt$.
items.pourquoi_faux: Segregation at meiosis puts only one allele of each gene into a gamete. A gamete cannot carry both alleles of the same gene.
items.correction_markdown: A $Tt$ parent produces two kinds of gamete, $T$ and $t$, in equal numbers.

items.erreur_markdown: In codominance the heterozygote looks like a mixture of the two parents, for example a pink flower from red and white parents.
items.pourquoi_faux: A uniform intermediate (blended) phenotype is incomplete dominance. In codominance both alleles are expressed separately and fully in the same individual.
items.correction_markdown: Roan cattle (red and white hairs side by side) and blood group AB (both antigens present) are codominance; pink flowers from red and white parents are incomplete dominance.

items.erreur_markdown: A cross of two heterozygotes carrying a recessive lethal allele gives a 3 : 1 ratio of normal to affected offspring.
items.pourquoi_faux: The affected class does not survive, so it cannot be counted among the living offspring. The zygotes are still formed in the ratio 1 : 2 : 1 but the lethal class dies.
items.correction_markdown: Remove the lethal genotype and the survivors are in the ratio 2 heterozygotes : 1 normal homozygote, and the family is one quarter smaller than expected.

items.enonce_markdown:
In pea plants the allele $T$ for tall stems is dominant to $t$ for dwarf stems. A tall plant of unknown genotype is crossed with a dwarf plant.

(a) Name this type of cross and state its purpose.
(b) Give the genotype of the tall plant if the offspring are 52 tall and 48 dwarf plants, and explain your answer with a genetic diagram.
(c) State the likely genotype of the tall plant if all 100 offspring were tall.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) This is a **test cross**. Its purpose is to reveal the genotype of an individual showing the dominant phenotype by crossing it with a homozygous recessive individual.

(b) The dwarf plant is $tt$ and produces only $t$ gametes. Dwarf offspring ($tt$) can arise only if the tall parent also gave a $t$ gamete. Offspring in about the ratio 1 tall : 1 dwarf (52 : 48) show that the tall plant produces $T$ and $t$ gametes in equal numbers. Its genotype is **$Tt$**.

| | $t$ | $t$ |
|---|---|---|
| $T$ | $Tt$ | $Tt$ |
| $t$ | $tt$ | $tt$ |

Offspring: $1\,Tt$ (tall) : $1\,tt$ (dwarf); 100 offspring would give 50 : 50, and 52 : 48 fits this expectation.

(c) If all 100 offspring are tall, the tall parent most likely produces only $T$ gametes, so it is **$TT$** (homozygous dominant) and all offspring are $Tt$.

items.enonce_markdown:
In the four o'clock plant, flower colour shows incomplete dominance: $C^RC^R$ is red, $C^RC^W$ is pink and $C^WC^W$ is white.

(a) Two pink-flowered plants are crossed and 200 seedlings grow to flowering. Give the expected numbers of each colour.
(b) A red-flowered plant is crossed with a pink-flowered plant. State the expected genotype and phenotype ratios.
(c) A gardener wants to start a pure-breeding line of pink-flowered plants. Explain whether this is possible.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Pink $\times$ pink is $C^RC^W \times C^RC^W$, giving $1\,C^RC^R : 2\,C^RC^W : 1\,C^WC^W$. Of 200 seedlings: red $= 200 \times \frac{1}{4} =$ **50**, pink $= 200 \times \frac{2}{4} =$ **100**, white $= 200 \times \frac{1}{4} =$ **50**.

(b) Red $\times$ pink is $C^RC^R \times C^RC^W$. The red plant gives only $C^R$ gametes; the pink plant gives $C^R$ and $C^W$ equally. Offspring genotypes: $1\,C^RC^R : 1\,C^RC^W$, which is **1 red : 1 pink**.

(c) **It is not possible.** Pink is the heterozygous phenotype. A cross between two pink plants always produces red and white plants as well, because the two alleles segregate at meiosis, so a pink line cannot breed true. Pink plants can only be made reliably by crossing a red plant with a white plant.

items.enonce_markdown:
A woman of blood group A has a child of blood group O. Two men are suggested as the father: man 1 is group AB and man 2 is group B.

(a) Deduce the genotype of the woman and explain your reasoning.
(b) Decide whether each man could be the father, giving genotypes.
(c) If the woman and man 2 (genotype shown in your answer) have more children, calculate the probability that the next child is group AB, and the probability that the next two children are both group O.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) A group O child has genotype $ii$, so it received an $i$ allele from each parent. The woman is group A, so she carries $I^A$ as well. Her genotype is **$I^Ai$**.

(b) Man 1 is group AB ($I^AI^B$). He has no $i$ allele, so he cannot give the child an $i$ and **cannot be the father**. Man 2 is group B, genotype $I^BI^B$ or $I^Bi$. The child needs an $i$ from him, so man 2 can be the father only if he is **$I^Bi$**.

(c) $I^Ai \times I^Bi$ gives gametes $I^A$, $i$ and $I^B$, $i$, so the offspring are $I^AI^B$ (AB), $I^Ai$ (A), $I^Bi$ (B) and $ii$ (O) in equal numbers. The probability of group AB is **$\frac{1}{4}$**. For group O the probability is $\frac{1}{4}$ for each child; the children are independent, so for two children it is $\frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{4} =$ **$\frac{1}{16}$**.

items_markdown: A gamete carries one allele of each gene because alleles segregate at meiosis; a monohybrid cross of two heterozygotes gives a 1 : 2 : 1 genotype ratio and a 3 : 1 phenotype ratio when one allele is fully dominant.
A test cross with a homozygous recessive reveals an unknown genotype: 1 : 1 offspring mean the tested parent was heterozygous.
Codominance: both alleles are expressed fully and separately (roan cattle, blood group AB). Incomplete dominance: an intermediate phenotype (pink flowers) and a 1 : 2 : 1 phenotype ratio.
A lethal allele kills the homozygous class, so the survivors show a 2 : 1 ratio and the litter is one quarter smaller than expected; this is why the result departs from the normal Mendelian ratio.
Always give a full genetic diagram: parental phenotypes and genotypes, gametes, offspring genotypes and phenotypes, with symbols defined and ratios stated.
